newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo economy faces bleak prospects without reform.
newsitem.headline: Yugo economy faces bleak prospects without reform.

text.p: Yugoslavia's economic policy faces a tough choice of radical reform or remaining passive and letting the entire system collapse, an economic think-tank warned on Tuesday.
Presenting its latest monthly report, the Institute of Economic Sciences (IEN) said it was vital for the government to reach consensus with workers on future economic programme.

"The first most important thing is to reach consensus among economists. But later, no government could apply any economic programme without agreement with workers. If not, workers will be on the streets," IEN economist Stojan Stamenkovic said.
"We hope there is an increasing need for reform, and that such a need will produce an atmosphere ripe for changes," IEN managing director Tomislav Popovic said.
Yugoslavia's economic prospects are obviously gloomy and range between recession and stagflation, he said.
Economic architects made two tremendous mistakes -- they allowed strong monetary expansion and did not prevent trade gap from surging to well over two billion dollars, economists said.
"All pieces have come together. The 1996 economic policy is completed, particularly in the second half of the year, to create an impression of success and good prospects.

"The entire policy was based on monetary expansion. Another problem was that imports and exports began to fall in November and December. It was very disturbing to see raw-material imports declining and imports of consumer goods soaring," Stamenkovic said.

The result was a large two percent month-on-month decline in December industry output and economic policy found itself once again in a position to choose between supporting the industry or halting prices.
According to IEN report, M1 money supply expanded by 500 million dinars in December, to top 5.5 billion dinars at the end of 1996. This was 69 percent above the December 1995 level.
In December, NBY extended credits worth 644 million dinars and the entire amount went to commercial banks. This was the way to cover their deliberately produced imbalances, IEN said.
All this has happened in times of fierce political tension and made it sensible to move from dinars to hard currency.

But despite the monetary expansion, companies remained illiquid. In other words instead to financing their production, dinars went on the streets, to buy hard currency, and this destroyed the only stable pillar of the Yugoslav economy -- its dinar, Stamenkovic said.
Popovic warned the situation could deteriorate if so-called unofficial forex reserves -- hard currency deposits kept by Yugoslav banks and companies abroad, begin to disappear.
Those were used heavily in 1996 to finance at least half of Yugoslavia's burgeoning trade gap. "If it happens, it could lead to fresh monetary expansion and hyperinflation," he said.
"All that has happened in December and January does not bode well for the economy in 1997, particularly with political tensions continuing," Stamenkovic said.
It is difficult for companies to be profitable now that the spread between the dinar official rate of 3.3 to the German mark and black market rate (at 3.9) widened to an almost 20 percent, he added.
"Another disturbing fact is that the British banking group National Westminster Plc last week said it would no longer advise Yugoslavia in negotiations with its international creditors," he added.

A declining numbers of foreigners coming to Yugoslavia with international airlines signalled a decreasing interest for the country. "This implies fewer foreign funds. And without foreign capital, pressure will grow on prices and the dinar."
"Once again, economic policy will be forced to produce money instead of goods. Or, if it focuses on the dinar stability, recessionary pressures will grow," Stamenkovic said.
-- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
